title: "Is there a better time in the year to buy a house in Australia?"
date: 2026-10-31
categories: [Housing Economics]
description: "I want to know whether house prices in Australian capital cities are seasonal."
---

::: {.column-screen}
![Real estate boards in Rosanna, Melbourne, in 2026: one townhouse sold at a winter auction, the one next door is up for auction in spring.](images/melbourne_auction_2026.jpeg){.hero-image fig-alt="Two real estate agents' boards outside neighbouring townhouses in Rosanna, Melbourne. One is marked sold after an August auction; the other is still for sale."}
:::

In this analysis, I explore whether there is a better time in the year to buy a house in Australia. I use median prices of established house sales from the Australian Bureau of Statistics. As a first step, I strip out long-run price growth to see how each city's prices move within the year, and set this against plain quarter-on-quarter growth.

## House prices relative to trend and quarterly growth, capital cities

```{python}
#| label: capital-prices
#| echo: false

import sys

import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from IPython.display import Markdown, display
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

sys.path.insert(0, "../etl")
from housing_prices import SOURCE, CAPITALS, load_capitals

series = load_capitals()

# Percentage deviation from a centred 4-quarter moving average (2x4 MA). Unlike an annual
# mean, this also removes the within-year drift, which would otherwise read as seasonality.
# It needs two quarters either side, so each end of the sample loses two.
trend = series.rolling(4).mean().rolling(2).mean().shift(-2)
deviation = ((series / trend - 1) * 100).dropna()
# Quarter-on-quarter growth needs only the previous quarter, so it runs further at both ends.
growth = (series.pct_change(fill_method=None) * 100).dropna(how="all")
# The quarter bands span every quarter that has either line.
quarters = growth.index.union(deviation.index)

LINES = {
    "Deviation from trend": (deviation, "#08306b"),
    "Quarter-on-quarter growth": (growth, "#e66101"),
}

QUARTER_BANDS = {
    "Q1 (Mar)": "#ffffff", "Q2 (Jun)": "#eeeeee", "Q3 (Sep)": "#d9d9d9", "Q4 (Dec)": "#bdbdbd",
}
# One heatmap per panel draws the quarter bands: cells are centred on each observation, so a
# point sits inside its own quarter, and it stays fast where 750 shapes would make zoom lag.
band_colours = [
    [bound, shade]
    for i, shade in enumerate(QUARTER_BANDS.values())
    for bound in (i / 4, (i + 1) / 4)
]

fig = make_subplots(
    rows=8, cols=1, shared_xaxes=True, vertical_spacing=0.03, subplot_titles=CAPITALS,
)
for row, city in enumerate(CAPITALS, start=1):
    both = pd.concat([deviation[city], growth[city]])
    low, high = both.min(), both.max()
    padding = 0.05 * (high - low)
    y_range = [low - padding, high + padding]
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Heatmap(
            x=quarters, y=y_range, z=[quarters.quarter] * 2,
            zmin=0.5, zmax=4.5, colorscale=band_colours,
            showscale=False, hoverinfo="skip",
        ),
        row=row, col=1,
    )
    for name, (data, colour) in LINES.items():
        fig.add_trace(
            go.Scatter(
                x=data.index, y=data[city], mode="lines", name=name,
                line={"color": colour, "width": 1.5},
                legendgroup=name, legendrank=1, showlegend=row == 1,
                hovertemplate="Q%{x|%q %Y}<br>%{y:.1f}%",
            ),
            row=row, col=1,
        )
    fig.update_yaxes(range=y_range, row=row, col=1)
fig.add_hline(y=0, line={"color": "black", "width": 0.8})

# Empty traces supply the quarter legend, because the heatmaps have no legend entries.
for label, shade in QUARTER_BANDS.items():
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[None], y=[None], mode="markers", name=label,
        marker={
            "symbol": "square", "size": 13, "color": shade,
            "line": {"color": "#999999", "width": 1},
        },
    ))

fig.update_xaxes(
    dtick="M12", tickformat="%Y", tickangle=-90, ticks="outside", showgrid=False,
    showline=True, linecolor="black", mirror=True,
)
# A fixed y-range makes dragging zoom along time only, keeping every panel's scale.
fig.update_yaxes(
    nticks=5, ticks="outside", showgrid=False, zeroline=False, showline=True,
    linecolor="black", mirror=True, fixedrange=True,
)
fig.update_annotations(x=0, xanchor="left", font_size=14)
fig.add_annotation(
    text="Per cent", textangle=-90, showarrow=False,
    xref="paper", yref="paper", x=0, y=0.5, xshift=-45, font_size=14,
)
fig.update_layout(
    height=1150, margin={"l": 60, "r": 10, "t": 90, "b": 50},
    template="plotly_white",
    legend={
        "orientation": "h", "x": 0.5, "xanchor": "center", "y": 1, "yanchor": "top",
        "yref": "container", "itemclick": False, "itemdoubleclick": False,
    },
)
fig.show(config={
    "displayModeBar": True,
    "displaylogo": False,
    "modeBarButtons": [["zoomIn2d", "zoomOut2d", "autoScale2d"]],
})

display(Markdown(
    "*Median price of established houses sold in each capital city: as a percentage above "
    "or below its trend (blue), and as a percentage change from the previous quarter "
    "(orange). The trend is a centred 4-quarter moving average, which smooths out "
    "seasonal swings and long-run price growth, so the first and last two quarters of the "
    f"data have no trend (the blue line ends in the {deviation.index.max():%B %Y} quarter). "
    "Vertical scales differ by city. "
    f"Source: {SOURCE}.*"
))
```

## Is the pattern statistically significant?

```{python}
#| label: x13-tests
#| echo: false

from housing_seasonality import FACTORS_FILE, TESTS_FILE

tests = pd.read_csv(TESTS_FILE).set_index("city").loc[CAPITALS]
factors = pd.read_csv(FACTORS_FILE, parse_dates=["date"], index_col="date")[CAPITALS]
by_quarter = factors.groupby(factors.index.quarter).mean().T
QUARTER_NAMES = {1: "March", 2: "June", 3: "September", 4: "December"}


def join(names):
    names = list(names)
    return names[0] if len(names) == 1 else ", ".join(names[:-1]) + " and " + names[-1]


def size(values):
    """A percentage, or a range of them if the cities differ."""
    lo, hi = f"{min(values):.1f}", f"{max(values):.1f}"
    return f"{lo}%" if lo == hi else f"{lo}% to {hi}%"


def swings(cities):
    """Describe the dearest and cheapest quarters of a group of cities."""
    group = by_quarter.loc[cities]
    peak, trough = group.idxmax(axis=1), group.idxmin(axis=1)
    if peak.nunique() == 1 and trough.nunique() == 1:
        return (
            f"{size(group.max(axis=1))} above the seasonally adjusted price in the "
            f"{QUARTER_NAMES[peak.iloc[0]]} quarter and {size(-group.min(axis=1))} below it "
            f"in the {QUARTER_NAMES[trough.iloc[0]]} quarter"
        )
    return (
        f"up to {size(group.max(axis=1))} above the seasonally adjusted price and up to "
        f"{size(-group.min(axis=1))} below it, peaking and bottoming in different quarters"
    )


# The two cities with the widest gap between their dearest and cheapest quarter.
spread = by_quarter.max(axis=1) - by_quarter.min(axis=1)
largest = [c for c in CAPITALS if c in spread.nlargest(2).index]
others = [c for c in CAPITALS if c not in largest]

passing = tests.index[tests["combined_test"] == "present"]
passes = (
    "Every city passes" if len(passing) == len(tests)
    else f"{len(passing)} of {len(tests)} cities pass ({join(passing)})"
)
dearest = by_quarter.idxmax(axis=1)
dearest_text = (
    f"The {QUARTER_NAMES[dearest.iloc[0]]} quarter is the dearest everywhere."
    if dearest.nunique() == 1
    else "The dearest quarter varies by city."
)

display(Markdown(
    "To test whether these swings are real seasonality rather than noise, I run each city's "
    "prices through X-13ARIMA-SEATS, the seasonal adjustment program used by the US Census "
    "Bureau and most statistical agencies, including the ABS. "
    f"{passes} the program's combined test for identifiable seasonality. {dearest_text} "
    f"{join(largest)} have the largest swings, {swings(largest)}. "
    f"In the other capitals prices are {swings(others)}."
))


def p_value(p):
    return "<0.001" if p < 0.001 else f"{p:.3f}"


rows = [
    "| City | Seasonality | Stable F (p) | Kruskal–Wallis (p) | Moving F (p) | M7 "
    "| Mar | Jun | Sep | Dec |",
    "|:--|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|",
]
for city, t in tests.iterrows():
    verdict = t["combined_test"].capitalize()
    factor_cells = " | ".join(f"{by_quarter.loc[city, q]:+.1f}" for q in range(1, 5))
    rows.append(
        f"| {city} | {verdict} "
        f"| {t['stable_f']:.1f} ({p_value(t['stable_p'])}) "
        f"| {t['kruskal_wallis']:.1f} ({p_value(t['kruskal_wallis_p'])}) "
        f"| {t['moving_f']:.2f} ({p_value(t['moving_p'])}) "
        f"| {t['m7']:.2f} | {factor_cells} |"
    )
display(Markdown("\n".join(rows)))

display(Markdown(
    "*Seasonality tests and average seasonal factors for the median price of established "
    "houses, by capital city. Seasonality is X-13ARIMA-SEATS's combined test for "
    "identifiable seasonality. Stable F and Kruskal–Wallis test for a seasonal pattern that "
    "is constant over time; Moving F tests whether it changes from year to year. M7 below 1 "
    "means the seasonal pattern is stable enough to estimate reliably. Mar to Dec give the "
    "average seasonal factor of each quarter, in per cent above or below the seasonally "
    f"adjusted price, over {factors.index.min():%B %Y} to {factors.index.max():%B %Y}. "
    f"Source: {SOURCE}; author's calculations.*"
))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Method

For each capital city, I run X-13ARIMA-SEATS (US Census Bureau, version 1.1) on the log of the median price. The program automatically selects a seasonal ARIMA model and detects outliers (one-off spikes, level shifts and temporary changes). It then estimates the seasonal factors with the X-11 filter. There are no trading-day adjustments, because the data are quarterly medians. As a cross-check, I fit the seasonal ARIMA order to the same log prices with `pmdarima`'s `auto_arima`, which chooses by BIC, the same criterion X-13 uses.
:::
